Is linux the go-to option or are there other good ones? Can the other OS be dual booted to make it easier for beginners?
Now that we all hate Windows, what OS should we use?

Linux has come a very long way. Most modern distributions operate very similar to windows for most common things. The every day computer user will not find linux any more difficult to go about their daily routines. For more advanced and administrative stuff there is still some mandatory use of the terminal but most common things have been better incorporated into the gui now so even those things are easier. Programs like wine and cedega allow you to install windows programs and games on linux and most run fairly well. Linux versions of new games are becoming more common because there are enough current linux users for major studios to consider support for linux. Unless you are using software or hardware that are extremely proprietary that do not have any linux support you could switch to linux completely. You would want to dual boot so you still had windows for those things.

The most popular distributions of linux are Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, SUSE, Puppy Linux, and Mint. With Ubuntu arguably being the most popular one with tons of support and an extremely active community.

If you want to try out linux without having to install it you can get a live cd and run from that. Most distros will have a live cd or usb option for new users. So you can try several different linux distros to see which one you prefer without ever having to wipe your drive and completely install each one which save you an aweful lot of time. Plus every linux distro will allow you to set up a dual boot configuration for people who dont want to drop windows completely.There are even a couple of different ways to set up dual boot as well.

Hope that helps you out.
Hey thanks a lot! I'll consider dual booting ubunto for a start!

My personal recommendation is xubuntu, which is a different desktop environment, a bit lighter, and, I think, behaves better, but I was a bit poisoned by the early days of unity (what ubuntu uses now, a bit like the ui change from win7 to win8+).

Whatever distro you choose, make sure to read up on some tutorials first depending on what your current version of Windows is. If you're on XP and possibly Vista and 7, then you should be able to just boot up with the Live Linux CD, explore a bit and when it's time to install, you can walk through the steps of resizing your Windows partition (be sure to defrag and scan for errors first, and make a backup of any important things just in case something does go wrong). If you're on 8/8.1, there are probably some things you'll need to do first. One, you're going to need to resize your Windows partition from within Windows as GPartEd has been known to screw things up. Then make sure you turn off Fast Boot (or whatever it's called) as 8/8.1 doesn't do a full shutdown, but more of a hibernation. If you try to access your Windows partition from Linux in this state, you run the risk of data corruption. You'll also need to turn off Secure Boot and possibly change from UEFI to Legacy BIOS in order to properly dual boot Windows and Linux. It might just be easier to install a second HDD just for Linux. I'm considering that route if I do upgrade to 10. Either that or only do gaming in 10 and use a VM for Linux and do all my regular work there.

For the sake of simplicity, I've been using Elementary OS. It doesn't have a whole lot of features beyond multiple desktops and window snapping, but most of what I use is within the Chromium browser anyway and it's the most aesthetically pleasing distribution I've used. https://elementary.io/
